diff_user.system: You are optimizing a Go function. Popcount(xs []uint64) int must return the total number of set bits across all words of xs. Each candidate is scored by running it in giri, a Go SSA interpreter, on 50 test vectors. It must return the reference result on every vector, and leave xs unchanged. Among correct candidates, a lower abstract cost (the number of SSA instructions executed over all vectors) scores higher, and any correct candidate scores above any incorrect one. The only import allowed is math/bits. Keep the function's name and signature.
responses:
## Proposed change: remove per-word bounds checks in the 16-word block

The score is the SSA instruction count, and the 16-word block is where most of the work happens for long inputs. Each `xs[i]` with a constant index emits its own bounds check (a compare and branch) plus the index computation. Every candidate so far has had the same cost (3549), so the remaining overhead is mostly in these repeated index and check operations.

Converting the slice once to a fixed-size array pointer, `(*[16]uint64)(xs)`, moves the check to a single length test at the conversion. Constant indices into a `*[16]uint64` are verified at compile time, so the 16 loads need no further checks. The conversion is safe because this branch only runs when `l >= 16`. The recursive call still receives `xs[16:]`, so the semantics and the "xs unchanged" requirement are preserved, and only the `bits` and math/bits import is used.

This is a targeted edit to the 16-word block only. The 8, 4, and tail ladders are left as they are.

Expected effect: fewer SSA instructions per 16-word block, which should lower the cost on the long-input vectors. The change is small and keeps the recursive structure, so correctness should be unaffected. If giri does not model array-pointer conversion, this would be a no-op rather than a regression, so it is low risk.
